Mr. President, excellencies, distinguished delegates, I have the honor to introduce the draft resolution A/80/L.105 under agenda item 13 entitled International Day of Greening the Planet on behalf of Armenia, Mongolia, and my own country, Kazakhstan. The initiative to establish this international day was put forward by His Excellency Mr. Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, President of the Republic of Kazakhstan, during his address to the 80th session of the United Nations General Assembly last September. Today, the international community is confronted with a range of interconnected environmental challenges. Climate change, biodiversity loss, land degradation, desertification, deforestation, water scarcity, and environmental pollution increasingly affect the well-being of our societies and the prospects for sustainable development. These challenges are global in nature, but addressing them requires practical action at the national and local levels. Protecting and restoring our natural environment is therefore not only an environmental initiative, but also an investment in the resilience, prosperity and well-being of present and future generations. Mr. President, against this background, the draft resolution proposes to designate 22nd of April as the International Day of Greening the Planet. The proposed observance is intended to encourage voluntary, inclusive, and practical greening efforts at the global, regional, national, and local levels. It also raises awareness of the importance of environmental protection and sustainable development. The initiative places particular emphasis on tangible actions that can be undertaken by governments, international organizations, local communities, civil society, and the private sector on a voluntary basis. Such actions may include tree planting, ecosystem restoration, urban greening, and land rehabilitation. While simple and practical in nature, these efforts can make a meaningful contribution to climate resilience biodiversity conservation, land restoration, and the creation of healthier and more sustainable communities. We believe that the strengths of this initiative lies precisely in its practical and inclusive character. Greening our planet is a responsibility that can unite countries and communities, regardless of their level of development, geography, or national circumstances. Dear colleagues, allow me to express our sincere appreciation to all delegations for their constructive engagement throughout the negotiation process. The draft resolution draws upon agreed language from a relevant General Assembly and ECOSOC resolutions and has been developed with a view to reflecting the interests and concerns of the wider membership. We are pleased that the text has successfully passed the silence procedure, demonstrating the balanced and inclusive nature of the draft and the constructive spirit in which the negotiations were conducted. I would also like to underline that implementation of the resolution have no program budget implications for the United Nations. Any activities associated with the observance of the International Day would be financed exclusively through voluntary contributions. We are grateful for the support this initiative has already received from member states, and thank all delegations that have joined the draft resolution as co-sponsors. We invite those Member States that have not yet done so to consider joining the co-sponsorship.

Mr. President, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, Many women around the world have suffered the bitterness of loss and the anguish of disappearance. Among them, Syrian women who have faced the worst crisis of missing persons in modern history. Today, we are proud that Syria has overcome a dark era where this pain was denied and the suffering of victims was ignored. It has moved towards the light. It acknowledges this tragedy, seeks to address it with full transparency, and mobilizes the international community to support those affected by it. In the past, this question was discussed in this hall in defiance of the Damascus regime. Today, however, it is discussed upon the request of Damascus itself. It was therefore both a duty and a solemn obligation that the first resolution Syria tabled in its new era be dedicated to this noble humanitarian cause. Colleagues, we fully recognize that the adoption of this resolution will not bring a missing person back, nor will it erase years of agonizing pain, uncertainty, and waiting, yet, It will enshrine the struggle of these women in the conscience of humanity and immortalize their efforts and the stories of their loved ones in the memory of the international community. It affirms that the world sees them, listens to their voices, and acknowledges the burdens they have borne and the sacrifices they have made in the quest to find their loved ones and uncover their fate. We extend our deepest thanks and gratitude to all the countries that supported this initiative, advanced its progress, and helped bring us to this historic moment, a moment where the international community, through a Syrian-led initiative, affirms its commitment to truth, justice, and human dignity, proving that as an international community, when we have the will, we find the way. We must not forget that many women were not merely searching for the missing people, they were among the missing themselves. For them, this cause is doubly personal. We solemnly remember the women who passed away before learning the truth. May this resolution serve as a tribute to their pure souls as well. In conclusion, I wish to address from this rostrum the women present here today and women everywhere. To every mother whose heart was broken, to every wife who waited endlessly, to every sister, to every daughter and female relative. To the women who, through years of hardship, bore the burdens of searching, waiting, and clinging to a thread of hope, and to those who refused to surrender despite the cruelty of their ordeal, demonstrating courage and determination. You asked questions when asking was an accusation. You sought answers when seeking them meant danger, and you kept faces in your memory when there was an attempt to consign them to oblivion. It is your courage, your steadfastness, and your legendary persistence that have brought this cause to this global stage. You have dedicated your lives to this cause. Yet this international day, which we seek to establish through this resolution, is truly your day. It is a day when we, as an international community, attempt to offer some measure of recognition for your tears and your patience. Thank you, Mr. President.

Mr. President, artificial intelligence offer significant opportunities for sustainable development, innovation, and entrepreneurship. Yet these opportunities are not equally accessible. Many developing countries still face gaps in digital infrastructure, connectivity, skills, education, expertise, and human capacity. These challenges can deepen digital and artificial intelligent divide. and limit the ability of countries to benefit from AI. The draft resolution therefore places capacity building and international cooperation at its center. It encourages partnerships to strengthen education and training. It promotes access to relevant resources, including open artificial intelligence models and systems, open training data and computing resources. It also supports the participation of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises in the digital economy. The resolution further calls for action-oriented international cooperation on artificial intelligence capacity building. Importantly, it promotes the meaningful participation of developing countries in AI processes. Mr. President, the resolution recognizes that effective partnership between governments and relevant stakeholders is necessary in developing approaches and frameworks for safe, secure, and trustworthy AI. It was on that day in 1955 that the proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project was put forward, the document that gave the world the term artificial intelligence. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Under President Trump, the United States is returning the UN to its core purposes and maintaining international peace through measurable results, not superfluous statements. Thank you, Mr. President. The present oral statement is made in the context of Rule 153 of the Rules of Procedure of the Assembly. The present statement will also be distributed to Member States. Under terms of operative paragraph two and three of the draft resolution, the General Assembly would request the President of the General Assembly, in consultation with Member States, indigenous peoples representatives and representative institutions, to organize within existing resources and on the margin of the 28th session of the Permanent Forum on indigenous issues, a workshop of not more than three days on enhanced participation open to the participation to all member states and observers of the General Assembly, indigenous peoples with accreditation to the permanent forum and to prepare a record of the discussions of the workshop as an input to the intergovernmental process of the General Assembly. and request the Secretary-General, within existing resources, to compile information from Member States and indigenous peoples from the seven socio-cultural regions on existing practices and acknowledgements of indigenous peoples' representatives and representative institutions and on possible barriers of participation, including inter alia, language barriers, accessibility barriers, technological barriers, financial constraints, and procedural challenges and examples of existing practices before the 83rd session of the General Assembly in support of the implementation of the resolutions. The request contained in operative paragraph two and three of the draft resolution would constitute additional workload for the Department for General Assembly and Conference Management, section two, and the Department of Economic and Social Affairs, section nine. For the Department for General Assembly and Conference Management, the request to prepare a record of discussions of the workshop as an input to the intergovernmental process of the Assembly as contained in operative paragraph two would entail additional resource requirements estimated at $24,500 excluding staff assessment in 2029 for a pre-session document with an estimated word count of 8,500 words in six languages the request within existing resources to compile information from member states and indigenous people from the seven socio cultural regions before the 83rd session of the general assembly as contained in operative paragraph three would have cost implications estimated at $17,300 excluding staff assessment in 2028 for a precession document with an estimated word count of 6,000 words in six languages and would be delivered to the extent that existing resources are available. For the Department of Economic and Social Affairs, concerning the three-day workshop in OP2, the note-taking and substantive preparation of a record of the discussion of the workshop would be undertaken within existing resources. regarding the request for in OP3 to compile information from member states and the indigenous peoples, the department would require consultations with member states and the indigenous peoples representatives and representative institutions across the seven socio-cultural regions, including the collection, processing and analysis of information from a broad range of stakeholders in multiple languages, as well as development of an appropriate methodological framework to ensure consistency and comparability of findings across regions. Implementation of these activities would require the engagement of consultations and individual contracts at an estimated cost of $179,000, $179,000 in 2027 and $89,600 in 2028 and would be delivered to the extent that existing resources are available, including through the mobilization of additional resources if possible. Should the General Assembly adopt draft resolution A/AD/107, Wherever the requirements are to be met within existing resources, every effort will be made by the Secretariat to meet the requirements within available resources, including through extra budgetary resource mobilization. And there would be no programme budget implications for 2027 and 2020, no programme budget implications for 2027 nor 2028. The Secretariat also wishes to inform the General Assembly that its ability to implement the mandate will depend on the availability of adequate liquidity resources. The requirement for 2029 would be presented in the proposed programme budget for 2029 for consideration by the Assembly during the 83rd session. Thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Under President Trump's leadership, the United States is returning the United Nations to its core purposes, maintaining international peace and security, and fostering cooperation among sovereign nations, as well as delivering measurable results, not ideological statements. The United States supports the preservation of cultural heritage and the empowerment of indigenous peoples through constitutional democracy and the rule of law. However, we voted against this resolution because instead of delivering practical localized results, the text seeks to build a parallel bureaucratic apparatus within the United Nations that attempts to grant non-state entities a quasi-sovereign status outside established intergovernmental channels. The United Nations is an organization of sovereign member states. Expending the organization's increasingly limited resources on mechanisms to accredit more non-governmental representative institutions would be contrary to the United Nations core purposes. This resolution locks the General Assembly into a multi-year loop of costly workshops, informal hearings, high-level panels, and newly appointed co-facilitators. This is UN process creep that consumes resources to sustain meetings rather than achieve tangible outcomes. True representation is achieved through transparent domestic democratic institutions, not through top-down sociocultural categories dictated by UN bureaucrats. The United States also notes the statement made by the Secretariat on the additional workload created by this resolution and emphasizes the importance of absorbing all additional activities within existing functions. We expect the United Nations to continuously exhibit this financial discipline as we continue to press for much needed reform of the organization. We underscore once again that U.N. General Assembly resolutions are non-binding documents that do not create rights or obligations under international law, nor do they change the current state of conventional or customary international law. The United States stands ready to work with any nation that shares our goal to restore the U.N.'s founding purpose and ensure it delivers real results for the nations and peoples it serves. We stand ready to cooperate on shared concerns, solutions, and reforms. Thank you.

This resolution represents an important step forward in advancing the implementation of the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and efforts to ensure that indigenous peoples can participate in UN discussions as distinct peoples and rights holders. We particularly welcome the practical measures contained in the resolution, including the workshop process, the appointment of indigenous advisors, the compilation of information on existing barriers to participation, and the preparation of a record for consideration by the General Assembly. Together, these measures will help inform future discussions on how to facilitate the participation of indigenous peoples within the UN system. While negotiations reflected a range of views, this process demonstrates a shared commitment to continued dialogue and engagement. The participation of indigenous peoples strengthened the inclusiveness, legitimacy, and effectiveness of multilateral decision-making. As implementation moves forward, we encourage all member states, indigenous peoples, and relevant UN bodies to remain actively engaged and to build on a momentum created through this resolution. We are pleased to support this resolution and we hope other member states will do the same. We look forward to continued progress on this important issue. Thank you.

The distinguished representative of India.

Chair, my delegation appreciates the presentation of the resolution on enhancing the participation of indigenous peoples representatives and representative institutions in meetings of relevant UN bodies on issues affecting them. India has consistently supported the rights of indigenous peoples and we remain committed to their active engagement in relevant UN meetings. For this reason, my delegation voted in favor of adopting this resolution. However, we would like to make the following observations. Despite extensive discussion, a lack of clarity persists on what enhanced participation would entail in practice, as well as on the underlying challenges facing indigenous peoples' participation that prompted this conversation. Amid the current liquidity constraints in the UN, it would be prudent for member states to ensure greater direction and clarity of objectives before advancing such mechanisms. It is pertinent to highlight the fact that for effective participation of indigenous communities, The biggest imperative is to identify them. Indigenous peoples must be defined based on internationally agreed standards, taking into account different national contexts as outlined in UNDRIP and reiterated by the PP3 and PP4 of this resolution. My delegation expects the spirit of these provisions to be respected and accounted for during the implementation of the resolution. We would like to reiterate that India adheres to the definition laid out in Article 1 of the ILO Convention No. 169 of 1989. It defines indigenous peoples as those regarded as indigenous on account of their descent from the populations which inhabited the country or a geographical region to which the country belongs at the time of conquest or colonization or establishment of present state boundaries, and who, irrespective of their legal status, retain some or all of their own social, economic, cultural, and political institutions. In India's context, we firmly note that the entire population of India at the time of our independence, including their successors till date, are indigenous. Thus, the international discourse pertaining to the understanding of indigenous peoples is not applicable to India. Therefore, it may be noted that the provisions related to indigenous peoples, especially those mentioned in OP1, OP2, and OP3, are not applicable to India. Thank you, Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of India and now give the floor to the Islamic Republic of Iran.

Thank you, Mr. President. The Islamic Republic of Iran has constructively engaged throughout the various phases of negotiations that led to resolution L107. Iran's position is grounded in its emphasis on the sovereign equality of states and the intergovernmental character of the United Nations. These red lines will continue to guide our position in any future consideration of the so-called procedural and institutional steps. Thank you.

In this context, we value the fact that the text adopted allows us to maintain this agenda on the General Assembly's agenda and to ensure the continuation of this issue. Mr. Vice President, my delegation voted in favor of this resolution, reflecting Indonesia's commitment to safeguarding cultural diversity and protecting traditional collective rights under our national legal framework. In doing so, my delegation deems it necessary to place on record the following interpretive statement. First, we warmly welcome the inclusion of the language derived from Article 46 of the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. reaffirm the paramount principle that nothing in this resolution or its implementation may be construed as authorizing or encouraging an action that would impair totally or in part the territorial integrity or political unity of sovereign states. Second, we reiterate that historical, regional, and national particularities vary across nations. As a nation where the entire population shares a common history of colonization and independence, And as a multicultural and multiethnic nation that does not discriminate against its people on any grounds, within our constitutional and legal framework, Indonesia recognizes and protects masyarakat hukum adat as subethnic communities, ensuring their traditional collective rights are respected. Third, while supporting enhanced participation, such efforts must remain firmly rooted within established intergovernmental processes. enhanced participation must complement existing modalities and strictly adhere to the rules of procedure of the respective UN bodies. Fourth, regarding the indigenous advisors, we expect them to discharge their duties in a transparent, objective and inclusive manner. It is essential that the advisors consult regularly with member states and thoroughly take into account the views and inputs of member states throughout the process. Finally, We emphasize that the implementation of all mandated activities must carefully account for the ongoing liquidity constraints and overall financial condition of the United Nations. Thank you, Mr. Vice President.
